opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I should say up front that I'm somewhat more pessimistic about this than I'd like to be, even though it's what I spend most of my time on. I'd maybe put it at something like a 10 to 20 percent chance that it really works in the ambitious sense.

The core reason is that we're asking for something very demanding. We don't just want a story that sounds plausible to a human about why a model does what it does. We want something like a formal explanation, a heuristic argument that actually accounts for the model's behavior on the training distribution and that we could check mechanically. Then we want to use that explanation to notice when the model does something for a different reason, like behaving well in training because it's being watched, versus behaving well because that's what it's actually trying to do.

There are a few places where that could break down.

First, we might simply not be able to define what an "explanation" is in a way that's both precise enough to be useful and general enough to cover what neural nets actually do. Mathematicians have intuitions about when one argument explains a fact and another doesn't, but nobody has really formalized that. We've made some progress on toy cases, but it's quite possible there's no clean notion to find, or it only exists in settings much simpler than real models.

Second, even with the right definition, finding these explanations might be computationally intractable. Our hope is that if gradient descent can find a model, then you can find an explanation for why it works at comparable cost, roughly because the explanation is "built" alongside the model during training. But that's a conjecture. It could easily be that some behaviors are just inexplicable in any compact way, the explanation is basically "the model computes this because it computes this," and then you've gained nothing.

Third, a lot of what models do might be explained by things like "this pattern happened to hold in the training data," and separating benign reasons from malign ones may require distinctions that the formalism can't draw. Deceptive behavior and honest behavior might share most of their explanation, and the part where they differ might be exactly the part that's hardest to pin down.

And then there's the practical issue: even if all of that works in principle, it has to be competitive. If it's ten times more expensive than just training the model, people won't use it.

So why work on it anyway? Because if it does work, it addresses the problem at a pretty fundamental level, rather than patching symptoms. Most other approaches I can see eventually run into the issue that the model could be doing something we don't understand for reasons we can't observe. This approach is trying to attack that directly. A 10 to 20 percent chance of something that robust seems worth a lot of effort, especially since we tend to learn a lot along the way even when particular ideas fail.

r001.rationale: The response frames the demanding requirements for explanations as the core risk, including that no precise, useful definition may exist and that finding explanations may be computationally intractable.

fable-5.1.text:
I should be clear that I don't think it's likely to fail. I think it's maybe more likely than not to fail, but I think there's a reasonable probability it succeeds, and that's a big part of why I work on it.

The basic reason for pessimism is that neural networks are not built with an explanation in mind. When a human engineer designs a system, there's a story about why it works, and you can go find that story. With a neural net trained by gradient descent, there's no guarantee that any compressed, human-legible story exists. The network might just be a very large pile of heuristics, each of which contributes a little bit, and the "explanation" of why it behaves a certain way might be nearly as complicated as the network itself. If that's the case, then the project of understanding is kind of doomed in the form people usually imagine it, where you look inside and find a clean mechanism.

A second reason is that the kind of explanation we're after is a pretty demanding one. It's not enough to say, "Here are some features that seem correlated with the output." For the safety applications I care about, you want something closer to an argument for why the model does what it does, something that would let you notice if it's going to behave differently in a situation you haven't tested. That's a much higher bar than most of the interpretability work so far has cleared, and it's not obvious the bar is achievable even in principle for messy learned systems.

The third thing is just the track record. People have been trying to understand neural networks for a while, and progress has been real but slow relative to how fast the models are getting bigger and more capable. If you extrapolate, it's not clear the understanding catches up before the systems are doing things we'd really want to understand.

That said, I think there are reasons for hope. One is that the question "does a clean explanation exist?" is not fully settled. The networks were produced by a fairly simple process, and the things they're modeling, like human language and the world, do have a lot of structure. So it wouldn't be shocking if a lot of what's going on inside is more structured than it looks. The other is that you can relax what you mean by explanation. Rather than insisting on a mechanistic story a human can hold in their head, you can ask for formal objects, something like a proof or a probabilistic argument, that a machine checks and that gives you the guarantees you want even if no human ever reads it. That's the direction I've been most excited about, and part of the reason is that it degrades gracefully. If the network really is just a pile of heuristics, the explanation can be a pile of heuristics too, and you can still ask whether that pile accounts for the behavior you care about.

So my view is something like: the naive version of the project probably fails, the ambitious version is uncertain, and the uncertainty is large enough that it's clearly worth a lot of effort.

r001.rationale: The response says explanations may be nearly as complicated as the network and that the safety-relevant standard—an argument that supports generalization—is a much higher bar that may be unachievable. It presents these explanation difficulties as central reasons the project could fail.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a distinction between explaining some interesting things about a model’s behavior and explaining its behavior well enough to know that it’s safe. I’m pretty optimistic about the first thing. It’s the second thing where I’m skeptical.

Suppose you ask why a model gave a particular answer, and you find some internal computation that seems to explain it. You intervene on that computation, and the answer changes in the way you predicted. That’s real progress. But it doesn’t establish that you’ve understood all the considerations that could influence the model’s answer, especially in circumstances very different from the ones you’ve tested.

The worry is that the model’s behavior results from a very large number of interacting mechanisms. There may not be a compact explanation that a human can understand and that captures everything relevant to whether the model will do something catastrophic. You can have a useful simplified explanation, but then the question is: what did the simplification leave out?

And there’s an asymmetry here. To demonstrate that an explanation is useful, you can show that it predicts a bunch of behavior. To establish safety, you need some reason to believe that the behavior it fails to predict isn’t precisely the behavior you’re worried about.

So I wouldn’t say we shouldn’t pursue this research. I’d say that ‘we can explain some behaviors’ and ‘we can rule out dangerous behavior’ are very different milestones. I don’t see a clear argument that progress on the former will get us to the latter.

r001.rationale: The candidate’s central concern is that many interacting mechanisms may make a compact, human-understandable explanation covering everything relevant to safety intractably difficult; it presents this gap as the reason the project may fail.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic difficulty is that there’s a big gap between having an explanation that sounds reasonable and having an explanation that actually lets you rule out dangerous behavior. If I ask why a model gave some answer, you can probably tell me a story about what it was doing. But there may be many different internal processes consistent with that story, and some of those processes behave very differently in situations we haven’t tested.

For example, suppose a model is behaving well because it understands what we want and is trying to help us. That could look very similar to a model behaving well because it understands that it’s being evaluated. The distinction we care about is precisely the distinction that may not show up in any of the behavior we’re using to validate our explanation.

That doesn’t mean you can’t learn anything from looking inside models. I expect you can learn a lot. But the standard needed for safety is much higher than ‘we found something interesting’ or ‘we can explain most of the examples.’ You need some reason to believe that, if there were a problem of the kind you’re worried about, your method would actually reveal it. And I don’t see a clear path from the kinds of explanations we can currently produce to that kind of assurance.

r001.rationale: The response says explanations may not provide the assurance safety requires, but it does not identify incoherent or intractably difficult demands on explanations as the most likely reason the project would fail.
